student: Welcome to AgentCore Runtime and Framework Integration. In the previous module we introduced the components of an agent and the AgentCore services at a high level. In this module we go deeper on where your agent actually runs. We will look at the open-source frameworks you can use to build agents, examine the core features of AgentCore Runtime, and see how to configure serverless execution with session isolation.

Here is our agenda. We'll start with the supported frameworks and how you implement an agent in them. Then we'll cover an overview of AgentCore Runtime and its features. Finally, we'll look at infrastructure and deployment. By the end of this module you will be able to deploy agents using supported frameworks with AgentCore Runtime, describe the core features of Runtime, and configure serverless execution with session isolation.
Let's begin with the frameworks you can use to build agents and how each one approaches the problem.

There are many open-source frameworks for building agents, and they all provide building blocks for tool use, memory, routing, collaboration, and production operations. We'll highlight four widely used options. The Strands Agents SDK is a lightweight Python SDK for typed, tool-using agents. It emphasizes safety through permissions, timeouts, and retries, and it embeds easily into backend services, which makes it a good fit for reliable automation and microservice tasks. CrewAI focuses on role-based collaboration, orchestrating teams of specialist agents with task decomposition, handoffs, review, and optional human-in-the-loop support, which suits coordinated content, research, and operations work. LangGraph and LangChain support complex, stateful applications; LangGraph models control flow as a graph with branching, loops, and checkpoints, while LangChain provides tool calling and memory, backed by a large community. These are a strong choice for multi-step workflows that need tracing and persistence. And LlamaIndex is data- and retrieval-first, offering indexes, retrievers, and routers so agents can query many data sources and synthesize answers, which makes it well suited to enterprise question answering and analytics.

Let's look at a concrete example using LangGraph. To create an agent you define four things: the model, the tools, the system message, and the graph. You start by selecting your foundation model through ChatBedrock, specifying which Bedrock model powers your agent. You then enhance the agent's capabilities by binding tools, such as a calculator and a weather function, using the bind_tools method. Next you craft a system message that defines the agent's behavior and acts as its foundational instructions. Finally, you construct the workflow using a StateGraph. You add nodes for the chatbot and the tools, then define the edges that control the conversation flow, including conditional edges that let the agent decide when to call a tool versus respond directly. The compilation step turns your graph definition into a working agent, with the entry point set to begin at the chatbot node.

Here is the same idea expressed with the Strands Agents SDK. To create the agent you define a system prompt, a model, and the tools, then pass all three into the Agent constructor. Strands operationalizes the agentic loop of reason, act, and iterate, so the agent can pursue a goal with evidence. It first understands your request and the available context, plans its next steps, and decides which tools to use. It then runs those tools, incorporates the results, and reasons again to refine its plan or conclude, repeating this cycle until it reaches a confident final response. Strands adds structure and safety to each step: tools have typed inputs and outputs, execution is permissioned and time-bounded with retries, and results are logged for observability. Once the system prompt, the model, and the tools are defined, the agent is ready to use.

Let's wrap up the frameworks topic with a comparison. There is no single best agent framework; each one is better for some applications. Strands offers a model-centric approach with minimal boilerplate, built-in multi-agent patterns, and production-ready observability optimized for AWS, though its model-centric design can feel less controllable and the community is still growing. CrewAI gives you clear role-based setup, strong short and long-term memory, and good documentation, but it is opinionated and can be harder to customize. LangGraph handles complex state flows and lets you bring your own agents as nodes, with a growing community, though it can be unstable between versions and its abstractions can break down in edge cases. LlamaIndex provides advanced retrieval and indexing with composable query engines and built-in evaluation tools, but its control flow often needs an external orchestrator and its performance is sensitive to index and embedding tuning. When choosing, consider how each framework handles failure and whether your use case can tolerate and recover from errors.
Now that you've defined your agent, you need somewhere to deploy and host it. That is the role of AgentCore Runtime, which we'll explore next.

AgentCore Runtime provides managed infrastructure built specifically for agents. Traditional serverless functions, like AWS Lambda, work well for stateless, short-duration tasks, but AI agents have very different requirements. Runtime addresses them by providing extended execution time for complex reasoning, by maintaining conversational state across interactions, and by offering secure isolation between user sessions. Unlike typical serverless functions that execute and immediately terminate, Runtime provisions dedicated microVMs that can persist for up to eight hours in asynchronous mode. This lets you build sophisticated multi-step workflows where each call builds on the accumulated context of previous interactions in the same session. And because pricing is consumption-based, you pay only during active processing, which keeps production deployments cost-effective.

Let's look at the core features of AgentCore Runtime. First, flexibility across frameworks, models, and protocols. Runtime supports multiple open-source frameworks, any model across Amazon Bedrock, Amazon SageMaker, or external providers, and protocols such as the Model Context Protocol and Agent-to-Agent communication. Second, session isolation, with persistent, dedicated execution environments for each session. Third, multimodal capabilities with large payloads: you can stream text, images, audio, and video bidirectionally, with payloads up to one hundred megabytes. And fourth, support for both real-time and long-running workloads, with fast initialization in roughly two hundred milliseconds for immediate responses, and long-running asynchronous workloads that can run for up to eight hours, enabling complex workflows like large document analysis.

There are three core concepts to understand in Runtime. The first is runtime and hosting, the agent hosting layer that runs your agent code and manages resource allocation, monitoring, and consistent performance. The second is endpoints and versions. Endpoints are addressable access points to specific agent versions, and you can create separate endpoints for development, testing, and production. The default alias automatically routes to your latest version, which streamlines your workflow. The third concept is sessions, which are isolated execution contexts for user interactions. Each session can run up to eight hours, giving agents time for complex reasoning, and the platform uses dedicated microVMs to keep sessions completely isolated. After fifteen minutes of inactivity, a session automatically cleans up, protecting user data and freeing resources.

AgentCore Runtime is not just for hosting agents; it can host agentic components more broadly. Agents, tools, and MCP servers can all run on Runtime, which provides integrated connections to essential services like Identity, Memory, and Gateway. Each Runtime session provides a hardware allocation of up to two virtual CPUs and eight gigabytes of memory. The benefits of this managed infrastructure are significant: you get support for any framework or model without infrastructure overhead, automatic session isolation for security and performance, and reduced operational complexity across a multi-agent system. In the architecture shown here, a client connects to a supervisor agent hosted in Runtime. That supervisor can call models hosted in AWS, interact with other agents hosted in their own Runtimes, and reach external tools and APIs, as well as MCP servers, through AgentCore Gateway. The key takeaway is that you concentrate on your agent logic while Runtime handles the underlying infrastructure.

Let's walk through how endpoints and versions work, starting with version one. AgentCore Runtime automatically versions your agent and lets you manage different configurations using endpoints. When you first create an agent in Runtime, it automatically receives version one as its default version. That initial creation also creates a default endpoint, giving you an accessible invocation point with its own ARN. When you make an HTTP call to the agent's invocations URL without any additional query string, it uses that default endpoint.

Now let's create a production endpoint. Beyond the default, you can create named endpoints for better organization and deployment management. In this example we create a new production, or PROD, endpoint and associate it with version one of the agent. The default endpoint also points to version one, since that is still the most recent version. To target the new PROD endpoint specifically, your HTTP call to the agent's invocations URL must include the qualifier query string.

Next, let's see what happens when we create version two. Whenever any part of the agent requires modification, including its role, its container image repository, or its container code, the system automatically creates a new version, version two. The default endpoint automatically moves to point at this latest version. Any other endpoints, like our PROD endpoint, continue to use the previous version until you explicitly update them. You can see the two invocation patterns here: a call without a qualifier hits the default endpoint, and a call with a qualifier targets a specific named endpoint.

Let's examine true session isolation more closely, because it is one of Runtime's most important security features. With AgentCore Runtime, each unique session runs in a completely isolated microVM, with its own separate compute, memory, and filesystem. When an invocation arrives with a specific session ID, the system creates that isolated microVM, so no session can access the files, state, or objects of any other session, whether it belongs to the same customer or a different one. This prevents a common class of vulnerabilities where temporary files or local state could leak between sessions. Sessions remain stateful within their boundaries, preserving in-memory resources for continued interactions using the same session ID. For state that needs to live beyond a single session, you use AgentCore Memory, which provides both short-term and long-term storage. This isolation benefits every use case, from routine commercial applications to sensitive financial and healthcare scenarios that demand strict data separation.

Let's look at the session lifecycle and its limits in more detail, keeping in mind that you should always verify the latest limits in the AgentCore documentation. Runtime manages sessions to optimize both cost and performance. Synchronous responses time out after fifteen minutes, while streaming responses allow up to sixty minutes. Each account supports up to one thousand active sessions in the US East North Virginia and US West Oregon regions, and five hundred in other regions, and this limit is adjustable. A session moves through several lifecycle states. It is active when it is processing a request or running a background task; background tasks are signaled when the agent code responds with a HealthyBusy status in its pings. It is idle when it has finished processing but remains available for future invocations. A session times out and terminates completely after fifteen minutes of inactivity, which you configure with the idle runtime session timeout. And a session can run for a maximum duration of eight hours while maintaining activity or health signals, which you configure with the max lifetime setting, used for asynchronous jobs rather than a single synchronous request. For applications that run longer than eight hours, the recommended pattern is to offload data to AgentCore Memory and reinstate sessions as needed, rather than trying to keep one session alive indefinitely.

Here is how asynchronous and long-running jobs work in Runtime. This matters whenever an agent needs to perform work that can't finish within a normal request-response cycle, such as data processing, report generation, or complex analysis that might take minutes or even hours. The benefit is that your agent can immediately acknowledge the user's request and then continue working in the background, so the user does not have to wait with an open connection and can check back later for results. Runtime manages this through the session lifecycle. Your agent reports its status through a ping endpoint. When it reports HealthyBusy, Runtime knows background work is happening and keeps the session alive; when it reports Healthy, the agent is idle and ready for new work. In the code shown, the SDK's API-based task management makes this simple: you call add_async_task when starting work and complete_async_task when done, and the SDK handles the status tracking automatically. Alternatively, you can implement a custom ping handler for finer control. Sessions can persist up to eight hours, giving you ample time for complex operations while maintaining context.

Let's bring it back to the agent you began designing earlier. Which Runtime features would you use when deploying it? Consider a few of the most relevant. First, framework and model flexibility, which lets you turn local agent code into a cloud-native deployment that works with LangGraph, Strands, CrewAI, or a custom agent, using any large language model. Second, session isolation and security, where each user session runs in a dedicated microVM, preventing cross-session contamination. Third, extended execution times for both real-time interactions and long-running workloads up to eight hours. Fourth, protocol support for the Model Context Protocol and Agent-to-Agent communication. Fifth, built-in authentication through AgentCore Identity, with support for both IAM and OAuth 2.0 for inbound access. And sixth, specialized observability with built-in tracing of the agent's decision-making. Beyond these, Runtime also offers automatic scaling, consumption-based pricing, support for one-hundred-megabyte payloads across modalities, and both HTTP and persistent streaming connections. All of this lets you focus on agent logic rather than infrastructure.
Now let's turn to infrastructure and deployment, and the different ways you can get your agent onto Runtime.

AgentCore Runtime supports two deployment models. The first is container-based deployment, which uses Docker containers and Amazon Elastic Container Registry. This gives you full control over the runtime environment through your Dockerfile, supports container images up to two gigabytes, and works with many languages and runtimes, which makes it suitable for complex applications with extensive dependencies. The process is to build your container, push it to the registry, and deploy it to Runtime. The second model is direct code deployment, which enables rapid prototyping by uploading a ZIP file, with no Docker, container registry, or build service required. Direct code deployment supports Python and Node.js, with a package size limit of 250 megabytes compressed and 750 megabytes uncompressed, and it supports custom dependencies through ZIP-based packaging while keeping deployment simple. In short, choose container-based deployment when you need full control and broad language support, and direct code deployment when you want to iterate quickly.

Let's look at the developer experience for getting started. Like other AWS services, AgentCore has a base API, split between a control plane API and a data plane API, which you can access using familiar SDKs such as Boto3 for Python. On top of those APIs, AgentCore also provides a specialized Python SDK with convenience methods that make integration much simpler. The AgentCore Python SDK offers primitives for Runtime, Memory, Tools such as the code interpreter and browser clients, Identity, and Evaluations, and it supports frameworks like Strands and LangGraph. If you use other AWS services in your agent, you combine the AWS SDK with your AgentCore SDK code. In addition, the AgentCore starter toolkit provides command-line tools and higher-level abstractions for deployment, for importing and migrating existing agents, for Gateway integration, for memory management, for configuration management, for observability, and for evaluations. Together, the SDK and the starter toolkit give you a smooth path from local development to production.

Here is how little code it takes to create an agent with the AgentCore Python SDK. The SDK is purpose-built for simplicity, requiring only four lines to produce a functional agent. You import BedrockAgentCoreApp, create an app by instantiating it, apply the app entrypoint decorator to your main agent function, and then call run on the app. You can implement any logic you like inside that entry point. When you deploy this code, it runs a server that exposes port 8080 and handles invocations for you, while AgentCore manages the infrastructure behind the scenes. Response handling supports both synchronous operations and streaming chunks, giving you flexibility in how your agent replies.

Let's see how the starter toolkit launches an agent, using a simple three-command workflow. The configure command handles infrastructure setup automatically, including creating the container registry repository for container-based deployments and setting up IAM permissions; if no execution role exists, it creates one with the appropriate AgentCore identity-based authentication. It also generates a YAML configuration file and, for container-based deployments, an editable Dockerfile that detects your entry point and dependencies from your requirements file. The launch command then deploys the agent to Runtime and prepares it for invocations, with typical deployments completing in under a minute for realistic agent containers in the five hundred megabyte to one gigabyte range. Finally, the invoke command prompts the agent using JSON payloads. Three commands take you from code to a running, invokable agent.

You can also create a Runtime agent without the starter toolkit, using command-line tools to configure and deploy manually. The high-level steps are as follows. First, enable observability for your agent by activating CloudWatch Transaction Search. Then install uv, a fast Python package and project manager. Next, define your agent code, which must include two endpoints: an invocations endpoint, which is a POST endpoint containing your agent definition, and a ping endpoint, which is a GET endpoint for health checks. After that, you test locally, create a Dockerfile that builds an arm64-compatible container with the proper dependencies, deploy the image to Amazon Elastic Container Registry, and finally deploy the agent runtime using the Boto3 client with the proper IAM role and network configuration. This path involves more detail than the toolkit, but it gives you full control, and the developer guide provides a complete walkthrough.

Let's compare the two approaches directly. With the starter toolkit, you get automatic container registry management, configuration abstraction that simplifies authentication and networking, deployment automation that handles building and pushing containers, and easy environment management for switching between development, test, and production. Without the toolkit, you gain fine-grained control with direct access to every configuration parameter, the ability to build custom workflows and integrate with existing CI/CD pipelines, support for advanced networking and security configurations, and room for custom enterprise authentication and monitoring integration. In short, the toolkit optimizes for speed and simplicity, while going without it optimizes for control and customization. Choose based on where your team is in its journey.

Let's recap this module. You should now be able to deploy agents using supported frameworks with AgentCore Runtime, describe the core features of Runtime including session isolation and extended execution, and configure serverless execution with session isolation. With your agent now running on managed infrastructure, we're ready to look at how to secure it.

That concludes the module. Take a moment to reflect on what you've learned about Runtime and framework integration, and how it applies to your own agent. Remember that AWS provides many resources for continued learning, including the AWS documentation, AWS Training and Certification, and AWS Support.
